item.title: Closed Network Operation and the Network Separation Transition
item.description:
Where this page fits

This guide covers the use and management of open source in the financial sector. Its starting point is the closed network. Import, internal mirrors, and offline vulnerability management are prerequisites for every stage, including identification, use approval, and management, so they are explained once here, and each stage page points to this page with an “Applying in a closed network” box.

Documents produced here: an import procedure and import approval records, and a self risk assessment for a network separation exception.

item.title: Self-Check Workbook
item.description:
This workbook turns the check items on the Self-Check page into a form for recording. Its purpose is to go beyond checking: for the areas that fall short, record the owner and deadline so that the results lead into an improvement plan.

How to use

Mark the compliance status of each item at one of three levels.

  • Not met: There is no related activity or document.
  • Partially met: The activity exists, but documents or records are insufficient.
  • Met: Both the activity and the supporting documents are in place.

For partially met or unmet items, write what the supporting document should be, and who will put it in place by when. For met items, write the name and location of the supporting document so that it can be used directly as verification material for ISO self-certification.

item.title: Governance: Management Organization and Approval System
item.description:
Where this page fits

Governance is the foundation of open source management. The identification, use approval, and management stages work only after you decide who is responsible, who reviews, and who approves. The FSEC guide also covers the composition and roles of the management organization separately, before the management procedures.

Documents produced here: an open source policy, a list of roles and responsibilities, and records of role assignments.

Where does financial sector governance start?

The “Guide to Using and Managing Open Source Software in the Financial Sector” (금융분야 오픈소스 소프트웨어 활용·관리 안내서; Financial Supervisory Service (금융감독원) and Financial Security Institute (금융보안원), 2022, hereafter the FSEC guide) presents the composition and operation of the management organization and examples of roles. ISO/IEC 5230 requires these as verification materials: a documented policy (3.1.1.1), a list of roles and responsibilities (3.1.2.1), identification of the people in each role (3.2.2.1), and a method for accessing legal expertise (3.2.2.3). Governance is the activity that produces these verification materials.

item.title: Policy and Procedure Templates
item.description:
The forms here are outlines that add items specific to the financial sector. For general open source policy and process forms, use the existing policy and procedure templates guide, and use the forms below for what the financial sector additionally needs: import control, risk assessment for network separation exceptions, and SBOM requirements for outsourcing.

How to use

The outlines below are not finished documents to use as they are, but frames to fill in. Replace the parts in square brackets to suit your organization. Have them reviewed by your internal legal and security teams before issuing them.

item.title: Identification: Finding All the Open Source You Use
item.description:
Where this page fits

Identification is the starting point of management. If you do not know what you use, you cannot manage its vulnerabilities or license obligations. It is the first procedure in the “Guide to Using and Managing Open Source Software in the Financial Sector” (금융분야 오픈소스 소프트웨어 활용·관리 안내서; Financial Supervisory Service (금융감독원) and Financial Security Institute (금융보안원), 2022, hereafter the FSEC guide) and the activity that SBOM management in ISO/IEC 5230 (3.3.1) requires.

Documents produced here: SBOMs and an inventory of production assets.

item.title: Audit Evidence List
item.description:
The financial sector must keep evidence of its open source management activities to prepare for internal and external audits and for information technology (IT) inspections by the Financial Supervisory Service (금융감독원). Because check records from the management step serve directly as evidence, do not create it separately; collect the records that come out of everyday activities in a systematic way. For more context, see Management.

Evidence checklist

The evidence below overlaps with the verification materials of ISO/IEC 5230 and 18974. Documents created while preparing for ISO self-certification serve directly as audit evidence. Set the storage location and retention period according to your organization’s rules.

item.title: Identifying and Resolving Issues: Vulnerabilities and Licenses
item.description:
Where this page fits

Once identification has shown what you use, the next step is to resolve the issues that come out of it. There are two kinds of issues: security vulnerabilities and license obligations. This is the second procedure of the FSEC guide, and it corresponds to vulnerability detection and resolution (4.3.2) in ISO/IEC 18974 and to handling license use cases (3.3.2) in ISO/IEC 5230.

Documents produced here: vulnerability remediation records (including VEX), and response deadline criteria by severity.

item.title: Tool Setup Recipe
item.description:
This recipe is an example of setting up SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) generation and continuous vulnerability monitoring in a closed network. As a quick starting point, it reorganizes the existing cdxgen and Dependency-Track pipeline tutorial for the financial sector. The purpose is not to recommend a specific product but to show how to build the setup with open source, on-premises tools.

Closed network assumptions

The example below includes a step that downloads tool images. In a closed network, obtain the images and vulnerability databases from outside, move them to the internal container registry and mirror, and configure the tools to pull only from inside. For the import procedure, see Closed Network Operation.

item.title: Practical Guide to Open Source Management in the Financial Sector
item.description:
Financial institutions use more and more open source, yet they must manage it under conditions specific to their sector: closed networks, network separation regulations, supply chain security, and audit response. This guide connects the management procedures set out in the “Guide to Using and Managing Open Source Software in the Financial Sector” (금융분야 오픈소스 소프트웨어 활용·관리 안내서; Financial Supervisory Service (금융감독원) and Financial Security Institute (금융보안원), 2022) with the verification materials of the international standards ISO/IEC 5230 and 18974 and with the existing KWG practical guides. It shows practitioners, in an actionable form, what they need to put in place and in what order.

Author : OpenChain Korea Work Group / CC BY 4.0

item.title: Usage Approval: What to Allow and on What Basis
item.description:
Where this page fits

This is the step where you decide whether to actually use open source that has gone through identification and issue resolution. Approval should not rest on one person’s judgment; it should follow a defined procedure and leave records. This is the third procedure of the FSEC guide, and it connects to license obligation review (3.1.5) and governance in ISO/IEC 5230.

Documents produced here: approval request, review, and decision records, and open source requirement clauses for outsourcing contracts.

item.title: Management: Continuous Checks and Audit Readiness for Internal Operational Systems
item.description:
Where this page fits

Checking once at adoption and stopping there is not management. Open source risk continues throughout operation, and new vulnerabilities are disclosed after adoption. This is the management (monitoring) step, the last procedure of the FSEC guide, and it corresponds to continuous monitoring in ISO/IEC 18974. It is the step with the greatest weight in the financial sector.

Documents produced here: periodic reassessment records, and audit evidence packages.

item.title: Self-Check: Finding the Gaps in Your Program
item.description:
Where this page fits

This page gathers the preceding six steps into a checklist. Go through the items one by one to find the gaps in your program, and move to the section that covers what is missing. The categories are based on the self-check checklist (Appendix 1) of the FSEC guide.

Documents produced here: the self-check workbook (check results and improvement plan).

How to use the self-check

This checklist is not a pass-or-fail test. It is a tool for gauging how far your organization has come and finding what to do next. Just as the FSEC guide is a non-regulatory voluntary check, this checklist is a best-practice baseline. [FSEC guide]

item.title: Artifacts: Ready-to-Use Forms and Recipes
item.description:
This guide provides four ready-to-use artifacts along with the main text. Where the main text explains “what to do and why,” the artifacts fill in “in what form to record it.” Each artifact is meant to be adapted to your organization’s situation.

Artifact Use
Self-Check Workbook Combines check items, ISO verification materials, and compliance status, owner, and deadline in a single sheet to find the gaps in your program
Policy and Procedure Templates Provides outlines for a finance-specific policy, an import procedure, a usage approval form, and a self risk assessment report for network separation exceptions
Audit Evidence List Organizes, as a checklist, the evidence required in internal and external audits and supervisory inspections and where it is kept
Tool Setup Recipe Provides an example of setting up and integrating on-premises SBOM and vulnerability tools in a closed network with docker-compose
How to use

The artifacts supplement the existing policy and procedure templates guide for the financial context. Use the existing templates for general practice forms, and use these artifacts together with them for items specific to the financial sector (import control, risk assessment for network separation exceptions, and SBOM requirements for outsourcing).
